name: Villanelle-Waste
geological_features: Repeating impact crater pattern from orbital debris
specific_features: Regular pattern of impacts suggesting orbital debris ring source
Surface features that are erased and recreated by ongoing bombardment
description: Villanelle-Waste is a small barren world trapped in a debris field that periodically resurfaces it through bombardment. The planet orbits through the remnants of a destroyed companion body, and each passage through the densest part of the debris field produces a rain of impacts that scars the surface in a pattern that repeats with each orbit. Old craters are obliterated by new ones, only to be recreated in approximately the same locations when the next bombardment cycle arrives, a geological villanelle of destruction and repetition.

The surface between bombardment cycles is a wasteland of overlapping impact craters, fractured crust plates shifted by the cumulative force of millions of impacts, and sublimation pits where volatile materials delivered by the impactors briefly exist before the next sun-facing rotation boils them away. The lack of atmosphere means impacts arrive at full velocity, even small debris producing disproportionate damage on a world with no buffer between space and stone.

The debris field is slowly dispersing, and models predict that the bombardment cycles will diminish over the next hundred million years until Villanelle-Waste's surface can finally heal. Until then, the planet exists in a state of perpetual renewal through destruction, its surface never more than a few thousand years old at any point. The geological record is effectively erased with each cycle, making the planet's pre-bombardment history unknowable through surface investigation alone.

Villanelle-Waste has no permanent value but serves as an occasional research target for impact physics studies, as the predictable bombardment cycles allow researchers to observe cratering processes in real time. Visits are carefully timed to the quiet intervals between debris passages, and even then, stray impactors make surface operations hazardous. The planet endures its recurring punishment with the patience of geology, each cycle the same verse repeated in a different voice, the refrain of stone breaking under stone.
